questions.question: Who was known as ‘Zinda Pir’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Aurangzeb**__.

• Aurangzeb was known as 'Zinda Pir', which means 'Living Saint'.
 
• He was the sixth Mughal emperor and ruled over most of the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Aurangzeb is known for his strict adherence to Islamic principles and his efforts to enforce Sharia law during his reign.
 
• He is often remembered for his military campaigns and expansion of the Mughal Empire.
 
• Despite his piety, Aurangzeb's policies and actions led to significant political and cultural changes in India.

• He was the founder of the Mughal Empire in India and the first Mughal emperor.
 
• Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the Battle of Panipat in 1526, establishing Mughal rule in India.
 
 
 
• **Humayun**
 
 
• He was the second Mughal emperor and the son of Babur.
 
• Humayun faced challenges in consolidating his empire and was temporarily ousted by Sher Shah Suri.
 
 
 
• **Akbar**
 
 
• He was the third Mughal emperor and is known for his policy of religious tolerance.
 
• Akbar expanded the Mughal Empire significantly and established a centralized system of administration.

questions.question: In cricket, which of the following is considered as LBW?

options.text: The fielder catches a batted ball on the fly.
The batsman’s body interferes with a bowled ball that would hit the wicket.
The bowler knocks over (or, breaks) the wicket with a bowl.
The fielder catches a ground ball and throws it at the wicket, knocking it down before the batsman gets there.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The batsman's body interferes with a bowled ball that would hit the wicket.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• LBW stands for **Leg Before Wicket**.
 
• An LBW decision is given when the batsman's body (excluding the hand) blocks a ball that would have gone on to hit the stumps.
 
• The ball must pitch in line with the stumps or on the off side for an LBW to be given.
 
• There are various conditions and interpretations by the umpire to determine if the ball would have hit the wicket.
 
• LBW is one of the ways a batsman can be dismissed in cricket.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bowled**

 
 
• This occurs when the bowler delivers the ball and it hits the stumps, dislodging the bails.
 
• The batsman is out bowled if the ball hits the stumps directly or after touching the bat or body.
 
 
 
• **Caught**
 
 
• A batsman is out caught if a fielder catches the ball on the full after it has hit the bat or the gloves holding the bat.
 
• This can occur anywhere on the field, including the boundary.
 
 
 
• **Run Out**
 
 
• A batsman is run out if at any time while the ball is in play, no part of his bat or body is grounded behind the popping crease and his wicket is fairly put down by the opposing side.
 
• This usually occurs when attempting a run between wickets.

• Typhoid is caused by the bacterium **Salmonella typhi**.
 
• This infection is primarily spread through **contaminated food and water**.
 
• Common symptoms of typhoid include **high fever, weakness, stomach pains, headache, and loss of appetite**.
 
• Diagnosis of typhoid is typically confirmed through **blood tests** that detect the presence of Salmonella typhi.
 
• Effective treatment generally includes the use of **antibiotics** to kill the bacteria causing the infection.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Other Bacterial Infections**

 
 
• **Cholera**: Caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, leading to severe diarrhea and dehydration.
 
• **Tuberculosis**: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs.
 
 
 
• **Protozoan Infections**
 
 
• **Malaria**: Caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted through Anopheles mosquito bites.
 
• **Amoebiasis**: Caused by Entamoeba histolytica, leading to gastrointestinal issues.
 
 
 
• **Viral Infections**
 
 
• **Influenza**: Caused by influenza viruses, leading to respiratory illness.
 
• **HIV/AIDS**: Caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus, affecting the immune system.

questions.question: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions or writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 32**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 32 of the Indian Constitution provides the right to individuals to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of their fundamental rights.
 
• It is known as the "Right to Constitutional Remedies" and serves as a guarantor of fundamental rights.
 
• The Supreme Court can issue various forms of writs such as Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari under this article.
 
• Article 32 is a fundamental right in itself, making it a crucial aspect of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar referred to Article 32 as the "soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 29**

 
 
• It provides protection of interests of minorities by ensuring that any section of the citizens residing in India having a distinct language, script, or culture have the right to conserve the same.
 
 
 
• **Article 30**
 
 
• It grants minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
 
 
 
• **Article 31**
 
 
• Article 31 originally dealt with the right to property, but it was repealed by the 44th Amendment Act in 1978, and the right to property ceased to be a fundamental right.

questions.question: According to the National Population Policy 2000, what is the target year for reaching stability in population?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The National Population Policy 2000 was formulated by the Government of India to address the issues of population growth and reproductive health.
 
• The policy aims to achieve a stable population by the year 2045, consistent with the requirements of sustainable economic growth, social development, and environmental protection.
 
• The policy includes objectives such as the reduction of infant mortality rate and maternal mortality rate, and promotion of contraceptive methods.
 
• It emphasizes universal access to quality health care services, including family planning and reproductive health services.
 
• Educational programs and awareness campaigns are crucial components of the policy to ensure informed choices regarding family planning.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)**

 
 
• IMR refers to the number of infant deaths (under one year) per 1,000 live births in a given year.
 
• Reducing the IMR is a key objective of the National Population Policy 2000.
 
 
 
• **Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR)**
 
 
• MMR refers to the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births due to complications from pregnancy or childbirth.
 
• The policy aims to bring down the MMR through improved healthcare services.
 
 
 
• **Contraceptive Methods**
 
 
• These include various methods and devices used to prevent pregnancy, ensuring family planning and reproductive health.
 
• The policy promotes the use of contraceptives to control population growth.

questions.question: Upon application of heat energy, the atoms of an ice cube start vibrating. At one point, the atoms have so much energy that they break away from their fixed position and loose the fixed structure. We can see this as the formation of water. What is this particular point called?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Melting point**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The melting point is the temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
 
• During melting, the atoms or molecules in the solid gain enough energy to overcome their fixed positions.
 
• The structure of the solid becomes loose, and the substance transitions to its liquid state.
 
• Melting point is a specific physical property of a substance, which can be used to identify and characterize it.
 
• In the case of ice, the melting point is 0°C (32°F) at standard atmospheric pressure.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Boiling Point**

 
 
• The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas.
 
• It occurs when the vapor pressure of the liquid equals the external pressure surrounding the liquid.
 
 
 
• **Decomposition Temperature**
 
 
• It is the temperature at which a chemical compound breaks down into simpler substances or elements.
 
• This process usually involves the absorption of heat.
 
 
 
• **Softening Point**
 
 
• The softening point is the temperature at which a material softens and deforms under a specific load.
 
• It is often used to describe the behavior of amorphous materials like glass and polymers.

questions.question: The concept of ‘Concurrent List’ in the Constitution of India is borrowed from ________.

• The Concurrent List in the Indian Constitution is borrowed from the Constitution of Australia.
 
• The Concurrent List allows both the Centre and State governments to make laws on the subjects listed within it.
 
• In case of a conflict between the central and state law on a concurrent subject, the central law prevails.
 
• The idea of a Concurrent List aims to ensure uniformity in administrative and legislative matters across the country.
 
• The subjects in the Concurrent List include education, marriage, bankruptcy and insolvency, and social security among others.

• Examples include defense, foreign affairs, atomic energy, and railways.
 
 
 
• **State List**
 
 
• The State List includes subjects on which only the State Governments can legislate.
 
• Examples include police, public health, and agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Residual Powers**
 
 
• Any subject not mentioned in the Union, State, or Concurrent List falls under the residual powers, which are vested in the Central Government.
 
• These subjects are not explicitly listed in the Constitution but are deemed necessary for the country's governance.

questions.question: Which of the following unemployment types is the result of people voluntarily leaving jobs in search of better ones?

__
 
• Frictional unemployment occurs when individuals voluntarily leave their jobs to find better opportunities or jobs that are a better fit for their skills.
 
• This type of unemployment is usually short-term and is a natural part of the job market.
 
• It can be beneficial as it allows workers to find positions where they can be more productive and satisfied.
 
• Frictional unemployment is often influenced by factors such as job search time, availability of information about job vacancies, and mobility of labor.
 
• It is different from other types of unemployment as it is not caused by economic downturns or structural changes in the economy but by individual choices and job transitions.

• Common in agricultural and informal sectors where surplus labor doesn't contribute to additional output.
 
 
 
• **Cyclical Unemployment**
 
 
• Results from economic downturns and is linked to the business cycle.
 
• Increases during recessions and decreases during periods of economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Structural Unemployment**
 
 
• Caused by changes in the economy, such as technological advancements or shifts in consumer demand.
 
• Workers' skills may no longer match the job requirements, leading to longer periods of unemployment.

• The term is derived from the Greek words "apo," meaning away from, and "Helios," the Greek god of the sun.
 
• Aphelion occurs for Earth around early July each year.
 
• During aphelion, Earth is about 152 million kilometers (94.5 million miles) away from the sun.
 
• The opposite of aphelion is perihelion, where the Earth is closest to the sun.

• For Earth, perihelion occurs around early January each year.
 
 
 
• **Elliptical Orbits**
 
 
• Planets orbit the sun in elliptical paths, with varying distances from the sun.
 
• These variations in distance are due to the elliptical shape of the orbit.
 
 
 
• **Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion**
 
 
• These laws describe the motion of planets around the sun.
 
• Kepler's First Law states that planets move in elliptical orbits with the sun at one focus.
 
• Kepler's Second Law states that a line segment joining a planet and the sun sweeps out equal areas during equal intervals of time.

• The Competition Act 2002 aligns with international standards of competition laws and aims to ensure freedom of trade carried on by other participants in markets in India.

• This Act regulates banking firms and ensures the soundness of the banking system in India.
 
• It does not directly address competition issues but focuses on the regulation and supervision of banks.
